lessonTitle: Asthma and COPD: Airway Inflammation, Spirometry and Drug Mechanisms

blocks.text: A 24-year-old woman wakes at 4 a.m. with a tight chest and a whistling wheeze. She has had the same symptoms after cold runs and around her flatmate's cat since childhood, and a few puffs of her blue inhaler abolish them within minutes. Her grandfather, a lifelong smoker, also wheezed, but his breathlessness never fully cleared with any inhaler. Both have airflow obstruction, but the cause, the reversibility and the treatment differ.

blocks.markdown: Airflow in the lungs depends strongly on airway calibre. Airflow obstruction arises when the airways narrow (smooth muscle contraction, mucosal oedema, mucus plugging, airway wall remodelling) or when the lung loses the elastic recoil that holds small airways open (emphysema). The two main obstructive diseases are **asthma** and **chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)**.

blocks.title: Asthma and COPD
blocks.text: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable, usually reversible airflow obstruction and airway hyperresponsiveness. COPD is a disease characterised by persistent, usually progressive airflow obstruction that is not fully reversible, most often caused by smoking; it includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema.

blocks.markdown:
### Pathophysiology of asthma

In atopic asthma, an allergen cross-links **IgE** on **mast cells** (a type I hypersensitivity reaction). Immediate release of histamine and leukotrienes causes bronchospasm and oedema. A late phase follows over hours, driven by **Th2 lymphocytes** releasing IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, which recruit **eosinophils** and drive mucus production. Chronic inflammation leads to airway hyperresponsiveness, smooth muscle hypertrophy, basement membrane thickening and mucus plugging.

### Pathophysiology of COPD

Cigarette smoke triggers neutrophil and macrophage inflammation. In **chronic bronchitis** (clinically defined as a productive cough on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 successive years), mucus gland hypertrophy and goblet cell metaplasia narrow airways. In **emphysema** (permanent enlargement of air spaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with wall destruction), neutrophil elastase and other proteases overwhelm the antiprotease defence, destroying elastin, so airways collapse on expiration and gas is trapped. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency removes the main elastase inhibitor and causes early, panacinar, lower-lobe emphysema, even in non-smokers.

blocks.markdown:
### Spirometry

Spirometry measures the **forced vital capacity (FVC)**, the total volume exhaled forcefully after a full inspiration, and the **forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1)**, the volume exhaled in the first second. In obstruction, airflow is slowed so FEV1 is reduced proportionally more than FVC, and the **FEV1/FVC ratio** falls. A ratio below 0.70 is the conventional criterion for obstruction (some guidelines use the lower limit of normal). **Reversibility testing** repeats spirometry after a bronchodilator; a rise in FEV1 of at least 12% and 200 mL supports asthma, while COPD shows little change.

blocks.caption: Ratio of volumes in litres; below about 0.70 indicates airflow obstruction.
Percentage change in FEV1 after bronchodilator.

blocks.title: Identifying an obstructive pattern
blocks.prompt: A patient has FEV1 1.8 L and FVC 3.6 L. Is the pattern obstructive?

steps.text: Compare with the threshold of 0.70. The ratio is clearly below it, so airflow obstruction is present.
A reduced FVC would suggest restriction or air trapping, but the key discriminator is the ratio.

blocks.answer: The ratio is 0.50, which indicates an obstructive pattern.

blocks.title: Testing reversibility
blocks.prompt: Pre-bronchodilator FEV1 is 1.50 L and post-bronchodilator FEV1 is 1.85 L. Is this significant reversibility?

steps.text: Absolute change = 1.85 - 1.50 = 0.35 L, which exceeds 200 mL.
Both criteria are satisfied, so reversibility is significant and supports asthma rather than fixed COPD.

blocks.answer: A 23% (350 mL) rise, a significant reversible obstruction.

rows: Stimulates beta-2 receptors, raising cyclic AMP and relaxing bronchial smooth muscle; rapid relief
Same mechanism with prolonged action; maintenance
Blocks M3 muscarinic receptors, reducing cholinergic bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion
Suppresses airway inflammation by reducing cytokine and inflammatory cell activity
Blocks cysteinyl leukotriene receptors, reducing bronchoconstriction and inflammation
blocks.caption: Bronchodilator and anti-inflammatory drug classes (names are teaching examples, not advice)

blocks.title: Treat the inflammation in asthma
blocks.text: Bronchodilators relieve symptoms but do not treat the underlying inflammation. Asthma control depends on inhaled corticosteroids, and a long-acting beta agonist is not given on its own in asthma. In COPD, long-acting bronchodilators are central and inhaled steroids are reserved for selected patients.

points: Asthma is eosinophilic, IgE- and Th2-mediated airway inflammation with variable reversible obstruction; COPD is smoking-related neutrophilic inflammation with chronic bronchitis and protease-mediated emphysema and persistent obstruction.
Obstruction is shown by a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (below about 0.70), with significant bronchodilator reversibility (at least 12% and 200 mL) favouring asthma.
Beta-2 agonists relax smooth muscle through cyclic AMP, muscarinic antagonists block M3 receptors, and corticosteroids and leukotriene antagonists reduce inflammation.

questions.stem: Which feature best characterises asthma rather than COPD?

options.text: Variable, reversible airflow obstruction with eosinophilic inflammation
Progressive, fixed obstruction with alveolar wall destruction
Neutrophil-predominant inflammation caused by tobacco smoke
Chronic productive cough defining the disease

questions.correctOptionText: Variable, reversible airflow obstruction with eosinophilic inflammation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: asthma has variable obstruction and eosinophil- and Th2-driven inflammation.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: fixed obstruction with alveolar destruction describes emphysema in COPD.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: neutrophilic smoke-induced inflammation is typical of COPD.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: chronic productive cough defines chronic bronchitis.

questions.explanation: Asthma is a variable, reversible disorder driven by atopic type I hypersensitivity and Th2 eosinophilic inflammation. COPD is largely fixed and smoking-related.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old non-smoking man has progressive breathlessness. A chest radiograph shows hyperinflated lungs with basal predominant emphysema. What is the most likely underlying cause?

options.text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Allergic atopic asthma
Chronic bronchitis from occupational dust only
Excess alpha-1 antitrypsin activity

distractorRationale.a: Correct: deficiency leaves neutrophil elastase unopposed, causing early panacinar lower-lobe emphysema in non-smokers.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: asthma does not cause permanent alveolar destruction.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: chronic bronchitis is defined by cough and does not produce basal emphysema.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: excess protease inhibitor would protect against emphysema.

questions.explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin inhibits neutrophil elastase, and its absence allows elastin breakdown and loss of alveolar walls. Early onset in a non-smoker with lower-lobe disease should raise the suspicion.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old smoker has FEV1 1.4 L and FVC 3.2 L. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Obstructive pattern, since the FEV1/FVC ratio is below 0.70
Restrictive pattern, since FEV1 is reduced
Normal, since FVC is preserved
Obstructive pattern only if FVC is above 4 L

questions.correctOptionText: Obstructive pattern, since the FEV1/FVC ratio is below 0.70

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: restriction has a normal or raised ratio, not a low one.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the ratio is clearly reduced.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: no absolute FVC cut-off defines obstruction.

questions.explanation: The ratio 1.4 / 3.2 is about 0.44, which is far below the 0.70 threshold. Reduced FEV1 with a disproportionately preserved FVC is the hallmark of obstruction.

questions.stem: A patient is given salbutamol for acute wheeze. What is the primary mechanism by which it relieves bronchospasm?

options.text: Stimulation of beta-2 receptors, increasing cyclic AMP and relaxing bronchial smooth muscle
Blockade of M3 muscarinic receptors
Inhibition of cysteinyl leukotriene receptors
Suppression of cytokine gene transcription

questions.correctOptionText: Stimulation of beta-2 receptors, increasing cyclic AMP and relaxing bronchial smooth muscle

distractorRationale.a: Correct: beta-2 agonism raises cAMP and relaxes smooth muscle.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is the mechanism of ipratropium and tiotropium.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is the mechanism of montelukast.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this describes inhaled corticosteroids, which are slow in onset.

questions.explanation: Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist that raises intracellular cAMP in airway smooth muscle, causing rapid relaxation. It relieves symptoms but does not treat inflammation.

questions.stem: Tiotropium is used in COPD. Which description of its action is correct?

options.text: A long-acting muscarinic antagonist that blocks cholinergic bronchoconstriction
A long-acting beta-2 agonist that raises cyclic AMP
An inhaled corticosteroid that reduces airway inflammation
A leukotriene receptor antagonist

questions.correctOptionText: A long-acting muscarinic antagonist that blocks cholinergic bronchoconstriction

distractorRationale.a: Correct: tiotropium blocks M3 receptors, reducing vagal bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: salmeterol and formoterol are LABAs.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: budesonide and beclometasone are inhaled corticosteroids.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: montelukast is a leukotriene antagonist.

questions.explanation: Vagal cholinergic tone is a major reversible component of airway narrowing in COPD. Muscarinic antagonists block M3 receptors and so cause bronchodilatation.

questions.stem: A patient has an FEV1 of 2.0 L and an FVC of 3.2 L. Calculate the FEV1/FVC ratio (a dimensionless ratio, to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation: The ratio is 2.0 / 3.2 = 0.625, which rounds to about 0.63. This is below 0.70, so it indicates airflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A patient has FEV1 1.60 L before and 1.92 L after a bronchodilator. Calculate the percentage improvement in FEV1.
questions.explanation: The rise is 1.92 - 1.60 = 0.32 L, and 0.32 / 1.60 = 0.20, or 20%. This exceeds both 12% and 200 mL, so reversibility is significant and supports asthma.

questions.stem: Compare the pathophysiology of asthma with that of COPD (chronic bronchitis and emphysema).
markingGuide: Asthma: type I hypersensitivity, IgE and mast cells, Th2 cells and eosinophils
Asthma: airway hyperresponsiveness, bronchospasm, remodelling; variable reversible obstruction
COPD: smoking-induced neutrophil and macrophage inflammation
Chronic bronchitis: mucus gland hypertrophy and goblet cell metaplasia with chronic productive cough
Emphysema: protease-antiprotease imbalance, elastin destruction, loss of recoil and airway collapse
COPD obstruction is persistent and progressive with limited reversibility
questions.explanation: Asthma and COPD involve different cells and triggers, which accounts for their different time course and treatment response. Reversibility is the main clinical contrast because remodelling and tissue destruction in COPD are permanent.

questions.stem: Explain how spirometry identifies an obstructive pattern, how reversibility testing helps to differentiate asthma from COPD, and why the FEV1 falls more than the FVC in obstruction.
markingGuide: FEV1/FVC ratio below about 0.70 indicates obstruction
Narrowed airways or loss of recoil slow expiratory flow so less is exhaled in the first second
FVC is relatively preserved because with enough time the lungs empty, though it may fall with air trapping in severe disease
Reversibility: post-bronchodilator rise of at least 12% and 200 mL supports asthma
COPD shows little or no reversibility
questions.explanation: Obstruction slows the rate of emptying more than the total volume, so FEV1 is reduced disproportionately and the ratio falls. Reversibility testing shows whether the narrowing is dynamic smooth muscle tone or fixed structural change.

questions.stem: State the mechanism of action of a short-acting beta-2 agonist, a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, an inhaled corticosteroid and a leukotriene receptor antagonist, and explain why asthma maintenance treatment relies on an inhaled corticosteroid rather than on bronchodilators alone.
markingGuide: SABA: beta-2 stimulation, increased cAMP, smooth muscle relaxation
LAMA: blocks M3 muscarinic receptors reducing cholinergic bronchoconstriction
ICS: suppresses airway inflammation and cytokine production
Bronchodilators treat symptoms but not underlying eosinophilic inflammation
Inflammation drives hyperresponsiveness and remodelling so controller anti-inflammatory therapy is needed
questions.explanation: Each class targets a different part of the pathway of airway narrowing: smooth muscle tone, cholinergic tone or inflammation. Because asthma is fundamentally an inflammatory disease, anti-inflammatory therapy controls the disease while bronchodilators only relieve symptoms.
